title: Prefatio close: Arminian fabric; elect unto faith; Anglican defense
pass_a_gloss: And what is more to be lamented, from the Arminian school there have come forth new doctors, who try to shake the most well-founded doctrine of the catholic Church, and to build I-know-not-what new fabric of election and reprobation, plainly unknown to orthodox Churches. What the Papists assign to foreseen works, these think must be assigned to foreseen faith and unbelief: And so at last they think they have looked out for Divine justice, if before the foundations of the world were laid he is said to have elected only those whom he foresaw would believe toward the offered grace of calling, and would persevere in faith clear to the end; On the contrary, let it be stated that he reprobated only those whom he foreknew would repulse grace, unbelieving, and would die in unbelief. Fine theologians indeed, who introduce a man first justified by faith, and placed in the state of adoption and salvation, before he is predestined by God, or elected to salvation in Christ! Splendid heralds of Divine grace, who refuse to reduce the difference of good and bad wills in believing or not believing to the special mercy of God electing toward believers: But whatever this difference is, they strive to recall it to the contingent act of free choice in admitting, retaining, and exercising grace. How much better, and more fitted to the Apostle's mind, is Augustine the scourge of the Pelagians On the Predestination of the Saints book 1 chapter 17: God elected the faithful, but that they might become so, not because they already were. By electing he makes them rich in faith, as heirs of the kingdom. There was therefore after Pelagius arose the explained and ratified opinion of Augustine and of all Catholics accordingly, that human beings were elected not from works but unto good works, not from faith but unto faith. That is, those who are elect came out faithful and devoted to good works; they were not elected because such ones were foreseen by God as about to be. This doctrine must be defended in the Schools, this preached in the Churches. For when other Pontificals pour out the poisons of their errors everywhere, let us also with no less industry prepare salutary antidotes for our people. That saying of Aristotle is known, etc. Let us also count it shameful to grow mute in God's cause, when enemies of the truth with writings and clamors shout against us on every side. Lest therefore the contagion of neighboring error seize ours too at last, according to the measure of my thinness I will undertake the explanation of that most true doctrine which this Anglican Church has recommended to all her own to be embraced in the business of predestination. I will also refute as far as I can those sophisms by which adversaries strive to overthrow the sound doctrine of the Church, and to establish their new fictions.
pass_b_english: And what hurts more: from the Arminian school new teachers have come out who try to shake the catholic Church's most settled doctrine, and to raise I know not what new fabric of election and reprobation, wholly unknown to orthodox churches. What Papists assign to foreseen works, these assign to foreseen faith and unbelief. So they think they have secured Divine justice if, before the world's foundations were laid, God is said to have chosen only those he foresaw would believe the offered call and persevere in faith to the end; and, on the other side, to have reprobated only those he foreknew would refuse grace, remain unbelieving, and die in unbelief. Fine theologians indeed — who bring in a man already justified by faith, already set in adoption and salvation, before God has predestined him or chosen him to salvation in Christ! Splendid heralds of Divine grace — who will not trace the difference of good and bad wills in believing or not believing to the electing God's special mercy toward believers, but strain to refer whatever difference there is to a contingent act of free choice in admitting, keeping, and exercising grace. How much better — and closer to the Apostle's mind — is Augustine, scourge of the Pelagians (On the Predestination of the Saints 1.17): "God chose the faithful, but that they might become so, not because they already were. By choosing he makes them rich in faith, as heirs of the kingdom." So after Pelagius arose, Augustine and Catholics generally held and ratified this: people were chosen not from works but unto good works, not from faith but unto faith. That is: the elect became faithful and eager for good works; they were not chosen because God foresaw they would be such. This doctrine must be defended in the schools and preached in the churches. When Papal writers pour out their error's poisons everywhere, let us with no less care prepare antidotes for our own. Aristotle's saying is known. Let us also count it shameful to fall silent in God's cause while enemies of the truth shout against us on every side with writings and noise. Lest neighboring error's contagion seize ours too, I will, according to my slender measure, undertake to explain that most true doctrine which this Church of England has commended to all her people to embrace in the matter of predestination. And as far as I can I will refute those sophisms by which adversaries try to overturn the Church's sound teaching and to settle their new inventions.
source_text: Et quod magis dolendum est, e schola Arminiana prodierunt novelli doctores, qui fundatissimam Ecclesiae catholicae doctrinam labefactare conantur, & novam nescio quam atque orthodoxis Ecclesiis plane incognitam electionis & reprobationis fabricam exstruere. Quod Papistae praevisis operibus, id isti fidei & infidelitati praevisae assignandum putant: Et sic demum Divinae justitiae prospectum opinantur, si ante jacta mundi fundamenta eos tantum elegisse dicatur, quos ad oblatam vocationis gratiam credituros, & in fide ad extremum usque perseveraturos praeviderit; Ex adverso eos solos statuatur reprobasse, quos gratiam repulsuros, incredulos, & in incredulitate morituros praesciverit. Bellos scilicet Theologos, qui hominem fide prius justificatum, & in adoptionis & salutis statu positum, quam a Deo praedestinatum, aut ad salutem in Christo electum introducunt! Praeclaros gratiae Divinae praecones, qui discrimen bonarum & malarum voluntatum in credendo aut non credendo nolunt ad Dei eligentis specialem erga credentes misericordiam reducere: Sed quicquid hoc discriminis est, satagunt ad contingentem liberi arbitrii actum in admittenda, retinenda & exercenda gratia revocare. Quanto melius, & ad mentem Apostoli accommodatius Pelagianorum flagellum Augustinus de praedest. Sanct. lib. 1. cap. 17. Elegit Deus fideles, sed ut fiant, non quia jam erant. Eligendo facit divites in fide, sicut heredes regni. Fuit igitur post Pelagium exortum Augustini atque omnium adeo Catholicorum explicata ac rata sententia, homines fuisse electos non ex operibus, sed ad opera bona, non ex fide, sed ad fidem. Hoc est, qui electi sunt fideles & bonorum operum studiosi evaserunt; non quia tales futuri praevidebantur a Deo, electi fuerunt. Hanc doctrinam in Scholis propugnare, hanc in Ecclesiis praedicare oportet. Nam cum Pontificii alii errorum suorum venena passim diffundunt, nos etiam haud minore industria paremus nostris salutaria antidota. Notum est illud Aristotelis, &c. Nos etiam turpe ducamus in causa Dei obmutescere, cum hostes veritatis scriptis & clamoribus suis undique nobis obstrepant. Ne igitur vicini erroris contagio & nostros tandem corripiat, pro meae tenuitatis modulo suscipiam explicationem verissimae ejus doctrinae, quam Ecclesia haec Anglicana in praedestinationis negotio suis omnibus amplectandam commendavit. Refellam etiam pro virili illa sophismata, quibus adversarii sanam Ecclesiae doctrinam subvertere, atque nova sua commenta stabilire moliuntur.
